379.title: Richer isn't better
379.hook: "I'm richer than you, so I'm better" doesn't follow (Enchiridion 44)
379.howItsDone: People practicing Stoicism sometimes catch comparisons that jump from 'they have more' to 'they are better' and correct the logic, as in Enchiridion 44.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was two handles: take a hard thing by the side that can be carried. Your line was he's my brother.

A twenty-year class reunion. Name tags, a slideshow, and a low hum of measuring. Who has the bigger house. Who has the better job title. Who still looks thirty. Nobody says the next step out loud, but it hangs in the room: so they're doing better than me. So I'm less than them. Epictetus heard the same hum in his own day, and in section forty-four he does something unexpected with it. He doesn't preach. He checks the logic.
screen: `A TWENTY-YEAR REUNION.` → `BIGGER HOUSE, BETTER TITLE.` → `RICHER ISN'T BETTER.`

segments.voice: Two arguments fail, he says. I'm richer than you, so I'm better than you. I'm more eloquent than you, so I'm better than you. The conclusion doesn't come out of the premise. Two others work. I'm richer than you, so my property is greater than yours. I'm more eloquent than you, so my speech is better than yours. Those compare like with like: money with money, speaking with speaking. Then the hinge, one short sentence: but you are neither property nor speech. The comparison is real, but it compares things you have, or things you do. The jump from my things are bigger to I am better quietly assumes that you are your things. A Stoic says you're not. You're the one who uses them, who judges, who chooses. And this frees both sides. It takes the air out of the reunion bragging. It also takes the sting out of losing the comparison. Their house is bigger. Fine: that says something true about two houses, and nothing at all about two people. You can admire someone's skill, or envy their savings, and still notice that it doesn't follow. The same check works on the voice that says I'm worse at this, so I'm worth less. That doesn't follow either.
screen: `RICHER, SO BETTER? DOESN'T FOLLOW.` · `RICHER, SO MORE PROPERTY? FINE.` · `YOU ARE NEITHER PROPERTY NOR SPEECH.` · `IT FREES THE WINNER AND THE LOSER.` · then, large: `DOESN'T FOLLOW.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one comparison that's been running in your head lately, a salary, a body, a family, a follower count, and say the full sentence with its hidden last step: they have more, so they're better than me. Then break it the way Epictetus does: their things are more, true; so they are better? Doesn't follow, and you can rest there a moment.
Richer isn't better. Epictetus checks the logic: more money means more property, not a better person. You are neither property nor speech. Today's word.
Your line: doesn't follow. More property, more polish, and still not a better person. Day three hundred seventy-nine, done.

380.title: Quickly, not badly
380.hook: don't say someone bathes badly, say quickly, until you know his reasons (Enchiridion 45)
380.howItsDone: Some people practicing Stoicism describe other people's actions in plain, observable terms before making any judgment about them, as Epictetus suggests in Enchiridion 45.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was richer isn't better: more money, more property, not a better person. Your line was doesn't follow.

A man walks into the public baths, washes, and is out the door in ten minutes, while everyone else lingers over the hot water, the oil and the gossip. Everyone notices. And everyone has the same word ready: he bathes badly. Sloppy. Rude. Doesn't know how it's done. Section forty-five of the handbook takes that one word and swaps it for another. It's a tiny edit, and it changes what you're claiming to know.
screen: `EVERYONE ELSE LINGERS AT THE BATHS.` → `ONE MAN IS OUT IN TEN MINUTES.` → `QUICKLY, NOT BADLY.`

segments.voice: Someone bathes quickly, Epictetus says. Don't say he bathes badly; say he bathes quickly. Someone drinks a lot of wine. Don't say he drinks badly; say he drinks a lot. Why? Until you know the judgment behind what he's doing, how do you know it's bad? Maybe the quick bather has a sick child at home. Maybe he's late for work, or the water is cold, or he simply doesn't like crowds. You saw the speed. You didn't see the reason. Keep to this, Epictetus says, and you won't end up grasping some impressions clearly and then agreeing to others you never actually saw. Quickly is something you saw. Badly is something you added. The habit spares you a thousand small, confident mistakes about other people. A twentieth-century psychologist, Marshall Rosenberg, built a whole approach to hard conversations, which he called Nonviolent Communication, on a similar first step: separate what you observe from how you evaluate it. You came home at midnight is an observation. You're irresponsible is a judgment. Two very different teachers, a long way apart, each with their own reasons, both noticing that people can hear a description without bracing for a fight. A judgment usually starts one.
screen: `NOT 'BADLY.' 'QUICKLY.'` · `YOU DIDN'T SEE THE REASON.` · `SAY ONLY WHAT YOU SAW.` · `OBSERVE FIRST, EVALUATE LATER.` · then, large: `QUICKLY, NOT BADLY.`

segments.voice: Think of someone whose habits bother you: the coworker who's always late, the neighbor who mows at seven, the relative on the phone at dinner. Notice the word you usually reach for, rude, lazy, thoughtless, then try Epictetus' swap and say only the description inside: late, early, often on the phone. Notice what happens to the irritation when the judgment drops out.
Quickly. Epictetus' swap: say he bathes quickly, not badly, because you saw the speed, but not the reason. Today's word.
Your line: say what you saw. Quickly is seen; badly is added. See you tomorrow.

381.title: Show the wool
381.hook: sheep don't show the shepherd their fodder, they show wool (Enchiridion 46)
381.howItsDone: Some people practicing Stoicism avoid calling themselves Stoics or explaining philosophy uninvited, and try to let it show in how they act instead.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was quickly: say he bathes quickly, not badly, because you saw the speed but not the reason. Your line was say what you saw.

Somewhere tonight, someone who just finished a book on mindfulness is explaining it at dinner, while visibly not being mindful. Plenty of people have been that someone. You've been on this path a long time now, nearly four hundred days, and it would be natural to want to talk about it. Section forty-six of the handbook has a word for that urge, and then it gives a strange picture: a field of sheep.
screen: `EXPLAINING MINDFULNESS AT DINNER.` → `NEARLY FOUR HUNDRED DAYS IN.` → `SHOW THE WOOL.`

segments.voice: Never call yourself a philosopher, Epictetus says, and don't talk much about your principles among people who haven't asked. Do what follows from them. At a dinner, don't explain how one ought to eat. Eat as one ought. Socrates, he says, had so completely given up showing off that people would come to him asking to be introduced to philosophers, and he would take them. He let himself be overlooked, and didn't mind. Here's the test: when someone tells you that you know nothing, and it doesn't sting, you can know you've begun the work. And if talk among people new to all this turns to principles, mostly keep quiet. There's a danger, he says, of throwing up what you haven't digested yet. That's not a polite image. He means it not to be. Then the sheep. Sheep don't bring their grass back up to show the shepherd how much they've eaten. They digest the pasture inside, and what comes out is wool and milk. So don't show people your principles; show them the actions that come from digesting them. Talk is the grass. Practice is the wool. People can't use your grass. They can use your wool: a moment of patience, a gossip skipped, a promise kept without swearing. After nearly four hundred days, a good sign of this path may be something someone else notices in you, without you ever mentioning where it came from.
screen: `DON'T CALL YOURSELF A PHILOSOPHER.` · `SOCRATES LET HIMSELF BE OVERLOOKED.` · `DON'T THROW UP UNDIGESTED GRASS.` · `SHEEP SHOW WOOL AND MILK.` · then, large: `SHOW THE WOOL.`

segments.voice: Look back over this path, the words, the stories, the practices, and find one thing that has actually changed in how you live: not something you could explain, something you do, like a pause before reacting, a smaller portion, a kinder answer. That's your wool. Hold it quietly, without a word about where it came from.
Pasture. What a sheep digests quietly inside, giving back wool and milk, not the grass itself; show practice, not principles. Today's word.
Your line: practice is the wool. Grass is for digesting; wool is for giving. That's day three hundred eighty-one.

382.title: In secret
382.hook: if you live simply or drink only water, don't announce it (Enchiridion 47)
382.howItsDone: Some people practicing Stoicism keep their personal disciplines private, so the practice serves their own growth rather than other people's admiration.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was pasture: the sheep digest it and give back wool, not grass. Your line was practice is the wool.

Day four of a new habit. No sugar, or a cold shower every morning, or a run at six. And there it is, the itch to mention it. A casual line at lunch: oh, I don't eat sugar anymore. A photo of the sunrise from mile two. For a lot of people, half the pleasure of a discipline is others knowing about it. Epictetus saw this itch in his students, and in section forty-seven he names it, with a picture of a famous philosopher hugging a frozen statue.
screen: `DAY FOUR OF A NEW HABIT.` → `THE ITCH TO MENTION IT.` → `IN SECRET.`

segments.voice: Once you've trained your body to live simply, Epictetus says, don't preen about it. If you drink only water, don't announce at every chance: I drink water. If you want to train yourself for hardship, do it for yourself, not for those outside. Don't go hugging statues. That's a jab at an old story. Diogenes the Cynic, the ancient biographer Diogenes Laertius says, used to embrace statues covered in snow in winter, to toughen himself. Epictetus admired Diogenes deeply, but he knew how easily a hard practice becomes a public performance. His alternative: when you're very thirsty, take a mouthful of cold water, spit it out, and tell no one. A small, private test that nobody sees, and those last three words are the whole practice. A discipline you announce starts working for the audience. You get the reward early, in other people's admiration, and the habit quietly changes its purpose. A discipline you keep secret has only one job: to change you. A neighbor tradition says something close. In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus teaches about giving to the poor in the King James words: "let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth." Two teachers, two different reasons, each in its own house, and a shared picture: some good things grow best in the dark, like roots.
screen: `DON'T SAY: I DRINK WATER.` · `DIOGENES AND THE SNOWY STATUES.` · `SPIT OUT THE WATER. TELL NO ONE.` · `ANNOUNCED, IT WORKS FOR THE AUDIENCE.` · then, large: `IN SECRET.`

segments.voice: Think of one discipline you keep, or would like to: a walk, a fast, a kindness, a limit on your phone, a habit of prayer or quiet. Ask yourself honestly who knows about it, and whether you want them to. Then picture keeping it entirely to yourself, even when there's an opening to mention it.
In secret. Enchiridion forty-seven: train for yourself, not for those outside. Spit out the cold water, and tell no one. Today's word.
Your line: tell no one. Some of the best work is never seen. Until tomorrow.

383.title: Signs of progress
383.hook: the one making progress blames no one, praises no one, and claims to know nothing (Enchiridion 48)
383.howItsDone: People practicing Stoicism sometimes review Epictetus' signs of progress, especially blaming no one, as a quiet self-check at the end of the day.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was in secret: train for yourself, spit out the cold water, and tell no one. Your line was tell no one.

How would you know if any of this is working? Progress is easy to count with a language or a marathon: words learned, miles run. A calmer mind doesn't come with a counter. Epictetus' students wanted to know the same thing: am I actually getting anywhere? Section forty-eight answers them with a checklist, and it isn't the one anyone expects. Nothing on it about feeling peaceful, or knowing more. It's mostly about what you stop doing.
screen: `HOW WOULD YOU KNOW IT'S WORKING?` → `A CALM MIND HAS NO COUNTER.` → `SIGNS OF PROGRESS.`

segments.voice: The ordinary person, Epictetus says, expects help or harm to come from outside. The person on this path expects it from inside, from their own judgments. Then the checklist. The one making progress blames no one. Praises no one. Finds fault with no one. Accuses no one. Says nothing about themselves as if they were somebody, or knew something. When blocked, they look to themselves. When praised, they laugh quietly to themselves at the one praising. When criticized, they don't defend themselves. Such a person, he says, goes about like someone recovering from an illness, careful not to disturb something that's healing before it has set firm. Progress here isn't a trophy. It's a mending bone, and you walk carefully on it. The Stoics called this prokopē, progress, and the one making it a prokoptōn. Epictetus doesn't describe arriving. He describes someone on the road. You'll never be told you've arrived. But you can notice, on an ordinary Tuesday, that you didn't blame anyone for the traffic, didn't need the compliment, didn't defend yourself against the remark. Small, quiet, real signs. And notice which one leads the list. Not courage, not wisdom. Blame no one.
screen: `HELP AND HARM COME FROM INSIDE.` · `BLAMES NO ONE, PRAISES NO ONE.` · `LIKE SOMEONE RECOVERING, CAREFUL.` · `PROKOPĒ: SOMEWHERE ON THE ROAD.` · then, large: `BLAME NO ONE.`

segments.voice: Run Epictetus' checklist slowly, as a mirror, not a test: blames no one, praises no one, finds fault with no one, says nothing about being somebody, laughs a little at praise, doesn't defend against criticism. Which is closest to true for you lately, and which is farthest? Hold that one gently, like a bone that's still mending.
Prokopē. The Stoic word for progress, and the one making it. Its first sign, in Enchiridion forty-eight: blame no one. Today's word.
Your line: blame no one. Help and harm start from inside. Day three hundred eighty-three.

384.title: Live the book
384.hook: proud of explaining Chrysippus? better to live what he wrote, and keep your principles like laws (Enchiridion 49–50)
384.howItsDone: Some people practicing Stoicism choose a single principle from their reading and try to act on it for a day, rather than reading or explaining more.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was prokopē, progress, and its quiet first sign. Your line was blame no one.

There's a kind of person you meet at the gym. They know everything about protein timing, muscle fibers, the right angle for every lift, and they'll explain it to you at length. They rarely lift. Philosophy has the same person, and so do plenty of hobbies: the one who can explain the book better than anyone, and whose life looks nothing like it. In Epictetus' school, the books students were proud to explain were by Chrysippus. Section forty-nine takes aim at the explainers.
screen: `THE GYM EXPERT WHO NEVER LIFTS.` → `THE BOOK EVERYONE EXPLAINED.` → `LIVE THE BOOK.`

segments.voice: Chrysippus was the third head of the Stoic school, and the ancient biographers say he wrote more than seven hundred works. Epictetus' own joke implies he was hard to read, so a student who could explain him felt rather proud. When someone boasts of that, Epictetus says, tell yourself: if Chrysippus had written clearly, this man would have nothing to boast about. Then he walks it through. What do I want? To understand nature and follow it. I find out Chrysippus explains it. I can't follow him, so I find someone who can explain Chrysippus. So far, nothing to be proud of. Explaining is only the doorway. What's left is to put the teaching into practice, and that alone is something to be proud of. If all I admire is the explaining, I'm a grammarian, not a philosopher, explaining Chrysippus instead of Homer. And when someone asks me to read Chrysippus to them, I blush, because I can't show actions that match the words. The next section turns it into a rule. Whatever principles you've taken on, keep them like laws, as if breaking them would be a kind of sacrilege. And whatever people say about you, pay no attention; that isn't yours. So the fair question isn't how much you can explain. It's which one line you're actually living.
screen: `CHRYSIPPUS: BRILLIANT, AND HARD.` · `EXPLAINING IS ONLY THE DOORWAY.` · `I BLUSH WHEN MY ACTIONS DON'T MATCH.` · `KEEP YOUR PRINCIPLES LIKE LAWS.` · then, large: `LIVE THE BOOK.`

385.title: How long will you wait?
385.hook: you're not a child anymore, and Socrates became himself by attending to reason in everything (Enchiridion 51)
385.howItsDone: Some people practicing Stoicism return to Enchiridion 51 when they notice themselves postponing something important, and take one small step that same day.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Chrysippus: explaining him is only the doorway. Your line was actions that match the words.

Monday. That's when it starts. Or the first of the month. Or after the holidays, after this project, after the kids are older, after things calm down. There's a thing you're going to begin, and a date it's going to begin on, and the date keeps moving. Near the very end of the handbook, Epictetus stops giving rules and turns to his student with a question, aimed straight at that moving date.
screen: `MONDAY. THE FIRST OF THE MONTH.` → `THE DATE KEEPS MOVING.` → `HOW LONG WILL YOU WAIT?`

segments.voice: How long will you put off thinking yourself worthy of the best things, he asks, and never crossing what reason tells you? You've received the principles you ought to accept. You've accepted them. So what teacher are you still waiting for, before you start setting yourself right? You're not a boy any longer, he says. You're a grown adult. If you keep being careless and lazy, adding delay to delay, setting one day and then another for when you'll start paying attention to yourself, you'll fail to notice you're not making progress, and you'll live and die an ordinary person. So whenever something hard or pleasant, glorious or shameful, comes along, remember: the contest is now. The Olympic games are here. They can't be put off. Progress is saved or lost by a single defeat, a single giving way. The Greek word for contest is agōn, the word for the games. This, Epictetus says, is how Socrates became who he was: by paying attention to nothing but reason in everything he met. And you, even if you're not yet Socrates, should live as someone who wants to be. The week closes here, and every line in it could start today: doesn't follow, quickly, not badly, show the wool, in secret, blame no one, live the book.
screen: `WHAT TEACHER ARE YOU WAITING FOR?` · `NOT A BOY ANY LONGER.` · `THE CONTEST IS NOW.` · `LIVE AS ONE WHO WANTS TO BE SOCRATES.` · then, large: `HOW LONG WILL YOU WAIT?`

segments.voice: Name the thing you've been meaning to start, the call, the practice, the apology, the first page, and the date you keep giving it: Monday, next month, someday. Ask Epictetus' question, kindly but honestly: how long will you wait? Then find the smallest first step, so small there's no reason to postpone it, and picture taking it.
Agōn. The Greek word for a contest, the games that can't be put off; you're grown, and the contest is now. Today's word.
Your line: the contest is now. The games are here, and they don't wait for Monday. Day three hundred eighty-five, and a week done.
